html:
SMTO-DB-0009 — The database query must say how many rows it may return

GUID: 7318a7a6-d2e6-42b4-9b60-adfedc03c904
Slug: sql-limit-required
Domain: DB · Subsystem: db

What happened

  • SMTO only runs database reads that set a maximum number of rows, up to a fixed limit for this SMTO. This query had no maximum, or asked for more rows than allowed. No query was run.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. If the Task is still running, wait. SMTO usually adds a row limit and runs the query again. The error tells SMTO the largest number of rows it may ask for.
  2. If you need information about many rows, ask SMTO for a summary instead, such as counts or totals by month. A summary gives you the answer in a few rows and stays well under the limit.
  3. If you need the full list, ask SMTO to fetch it in pages, for example the first 500 rows, then the next 500. Each page stays within the limit, and together the pages cover everything.
  4. If you regularly need more rows in one go, ask the person who manages SMTO whether the row limit can be raised. The limit is set for the whole installation and only they can change it.

What success looks like

  • SMTO shows the results, or the first page of them, and says whether more rows remain.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO. Don't keep asking for the same large query; it will be refused until it sets a smaller maximum.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • A row-returning read query was rejected because it has no explicit literal top-level LIMIT, or its LIMIT is below 1 or above the configured database_max_rows.

What this means

  • A row-returning read lacks a recognized explicit limit, or its parsed top-level limit lies outside one through the runtime allowance. Input rejection is pre-dispatch only where the producer says so. Discovery and psql failures require their original execution evidence; diagnostics do not run SQL or prove that a mutation rolled back.

Why this can happen

  • A row-returning read lacks a recognized explicit limit, or its parsed top-level limit lies outside one through the runtime allowance.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the top-level literal LIMIT and whether this query shape requires one; count-only queries may follow a separate rule.

How to fix it

  • Add a positive literal LIMIT no greater than the allowance shown in the message (database_max_rows, from AOR_DATABASE_MAX_ROWS, default 1000). Fetch more data with ORDER BY plus keyset or OFFSET pagination, or with aggregate queries. An administrator may raise AOR_DATABASE_MAX_ROWS and restart the server, but must not remove the limit check.
  • Add a positive literal LIMIT no larger than the reported row allowance. Use pagination or separate scoped reads for additional complete data.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The bounded read passes classification and any additional data is obtained through scoped pagination.

What not to do

  • Do not repeatedly submit the same invalid input; correct the named constraint first.

Technical notes

  • Input rejection is pre-dispatch only where the producer says so. Discovery and psql failures require their original execution evidence; diagnostics do not run SQL or prove that a mutation rolled back.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
